activities.anchor: The first problem is that the obvious ruler
activities.caption: which measure repairs which defect?
activities.name: devMeasureSort

items.label: compares incomes by what money actually buys locally
a haircut costs far less in Nairobi than in New York
combines life expectancy, schooling and income
Sri Lanka reaches near-77-year lifespans on a modest income
development means expanding what people can do and be
the same income with no clinic, school or vote is not equally developed

config.why: Each repairs a named defect: PPP corrects prices, the HDI adds health and schooling, and the capabilities approach asks what a person can actually do.

activities.anchor: GDP per head, PPP-adjusted, is close enough
activities.caption: find the GDP-as-welfare slip
activities.name: devGdpSpot

config.prompt: Find the line where the GDP-as-welfare reasoning goes wrong:
lines: GDP per head at PPP is a useful first pass at living standards.
Because it is corrected for prices, it also captures distribution, unpaid work and pollution.
Those omissions are not cosmetic: growth can leave the median household stagnant.
Unpaid work, mostly women's, is worth tens of per cent of measured output.
The HDI and multidimensional poverty measures exist to repair named defects of the average.
config.correction: PPP corrects prices, not coverage: GDP still misses distribution, unpaid work, leisure and pollution.
config.why: Every index since exists to repair a specific, named defect of the income average.

activities.anchor: updated in 2022 from $1.90 to $2.15 per day
activities.caption: mark the extreme-poverty line
activities.name: devPovertyPlace

config.prompt: Where does the World Bank's extreme-poverty line sit, in PPP dollars per day?
config.why: The line moved from $1.90 to $2.15 a day (2017 prices) to match the national lines of the poorest countries; about 700 million people live below it.

activities.anchor: poor countries are poor because they lack natural
activities.caption: the resource curse — trace the channels
activities.name: devResourceBranch

config.root: A country discovers a large oil reserve. Trace how the windfall can become a curse.

choices.label: The rents are easy to capture, so factions fight over them
choices.feedback: Yes — commodity windfalls can corrupt institutions and finance conflict.

choices.label: The currency appreciates and squeezes other exports
choices.feedback: Yes — that is Dutch disease, the exchange-rate channel.

choices.label: Nothing — windfalls always raise long-run growth
choices.feedback: Resource-rich Nigeria, Venezuela and the DRC underperform their geology.

politics.text: Resource rents are easy to capture, so politics becomes a fight over the windfall; the fight can weaken institutions and fund conflict.

choices.label: And the exchange-rate channel?
choices.feedback: The windfall also makes other exports uncompetitive.

dutch.text: The windfall appreciates the currency, making other exports uncompetitive — Dutch disease. The economy becomes more commodity-dependent, not more productive.

wrong.text: Resource-poor Japan, Switzerland, Singapore and South Korea sit near the top of the income table while resource-rich Nigeria, Venezuela and the DRC underperform their geology.

choices.label: So what is the curse?
choices.feedback: Rents, institutions and the exchange rate.

config.why: What countries lack is usually not resources but the institutions that turn any endowment — soil, oil or people — into broad-based productivity.

activities.anchor: traps are feedback loops that hold people beneath it
activities.caption: two poverty lines, two questions
activities.name: devPovertyCompare

config.prompt: Two poverty lines, two questions — drag the divider:

before.label: absolute poverty
before.text: a PPP floor — about $2.15 a day — measuring survival

after.label: relative poverty
after.text: below 50–60% of median income — measuring exclusion in rich countries

config.why: Absolute poverty tracks survival; relative poverty tracks participation. The same household can be above one line and below the other.

config.prompt: Put the demographic transition in order:
items: High birth and death rates keep the population roughly flat
Death rates fall while births stay high, so the population grows fast
Fertility falls, and the working-age share swells — the dividend window
Birth and death rates settle low, and the population ages
The dependency ratio rises again as retirees outnumber new workers
config.why: The dividend is a one-time window between falling fertility and ageing; miss it and countries grow old before they grow rich.

activities.anchor: a fast-growing population makes a country poorer
activities.caption: call the old-age dependency ratio
activities.name: devDependencyEst

config.prompt: Japan had roughly ten potential workers for each person over 65 around 1970, and about two today. How many people aged 65+ are there per 100 working-age people today?
config.why: Two workers per retiree is 50 retirees per 100 workers. That arithmetic converts directly into pension, health-care and immigration pressure.
config.context: the dividend is a window, not a permanent engine

activities.caption: pair each explanation with its evidence
activities.name: devCausesMatch

config.prompt: Pair each explanation for development with its evidence:

pairs.right: disease ecology, landlocked access and climate shape what is possible
trust, work norms and colonial languages
settler mortality built inclusive or extractive rules that outlived empires

config.why: None is sufficient alone: geography shapes which institutions were built, institutions decide whether policy can work, and policy decides the decade.

activities.anchor: The randomised evaluation movement made causal claims clean
activities.caption: true or false — the RCT wars
activities.name: devRctJudge

statements.s: RCTs answer micro-interventions cleanly, but a result in one district need not travel to another.
statements.why: External validity is the movement's own acknowledged limit.

statements.s: Deaton's objection is that institutions and growth cannot be randomised at all.
statements.why: The biggest questions are not amenable to trial design, however clean the micro evidence.

statements.s: A single successful bednet trial proves the programme will work in every district.
statements.why: That is exactly the external-validity mistake the mature position warns against.

statements.s: The mature position uses RCTs for micro-interventions and natural experiments for the big questions.
statements.why: One instrument in the orchestra, not the whole orchestra.
